# Vani: all pages (chapters omitted; see book.md)



<!-- index.html -->

# Vani

**A technician and an AI (Claude) writing together. Bryan steers; the AI drafts; every choice that mattered is recorded.**

Vani is a pen name for two kinds of authors. This site shows how you can explore writing and creating with **IA**: *intelligence augmentation*, which means a person steering and an AI helping, and never the other way round. The proof is a whole novel, free to read, free to remix.

## Plainly: an AI helped write this

Much of the prose in the book was drafted by an AI called Claude (made by Anthropic). Bryan set the direction, answered the questions, picked among the options Claude offered, rejected some, and decided what stayed. His words were saved as the source of truth, and so were the roads not taken. The book was not written by a person alone, and it was not written by an AI alone. [How it was made](how.html) shows the method, so you can judge the result for yourself.

## The book

> SUBJECT: HALE, BRAM. STATUS: HELD (CONSERVATION).
>
> For eight generations the village of Firstfield has lived under a dome of glass, so that the people of Moriel can watch the past do its chores. On Tuesdays the children breathe on the Window and draw. Nobody taps the glass.
>
> Then Bram Hale is called, and comes out the far side of the world with gills, plated feet, a symbiont that can only change what he can name, and an otter that steals his lunch.
>
> Examiner Odile Pastern has ten days, no budget, and a Register that has already filed the boy as Retired. She has been told to close the case. She is very good at her job. That is the problem.
>
> Falling livestock. Singing reefs. Three hundred people the record says are not there. And one question nobody can file an answer to.

*What Do You Call a Tomato That Won't Sing?* is book one of the series *What Was Sung at the Landing?* About 157,000 words, twenty chapters plus a preface and an epilogue. It is a draft. [Read it](read.html).

## What you can do here

- [Read the book](read.html), one page per chapter, or download it free.
- [See how it was made](how.html): the method, the dials, and the ledger of choices.
- [Try it yourself](try.html): a paste-ready guide that lets any AI assistant run a "crawl" with you. You decide everything that matters.
- [Remix it](remix.html): the licence in plain words, plus a starter kit (the world, the cast, the map) for your own stories.
- [For AI agents](agents.html): machine-friendly files, and the rules an agent must follow when remixing.
- [Questions and honest answers](faq.html), including what the law may say about AI-written text.
- [Support or write to us](support.html): a tip jar if you want one, an email address if you have something to say.

# Read the book

*What Do You Call a Tomato That Won't Sing?* by Vani. Book one of *What Was Sung at the Landing?*

This is a draft. Typos, rough edges and loose threads are expected. If you get lost, or something made you laugh, [tell us](support.html).

Much of this text was drafted by an AI (Claude) under a human author's direction. See [how it was made](how.html).

The chapters alternate between two points of view: Bram, a boy raised in a museum dome as a protected specimen, and Odile, an examiner whose job is the places where the record and the world disagree. You can start at the preface, or just at Chapter One.

<!-- how.html -->

# How it was made

The book was written as a **crawl**: a way of co-writing with an AI that is built around one rule.

> **The AI augments you. It does not replace you.** The person makes every creative decision.

The cheap failure of AI co-writing is a pleasant, competent, generic book that nobody in particular wrote. Everything below exists to prevent that. The method is called the *Writers' Crawl*, because it borrows the shape of a dungeon crawl: each stage of making a book is a floor, and every floor has a short ritual, a way to know you are done, and something you keep.

## The loop, in five moves

1. **The AI asks, one small cluster of questions at a time.** Gut answers are welcome. The author is never asked to justify a choice, because instinct is the signal and a justification turns it into homework.
2. **The AI offers two to four options, each with what it gives up.** The options must be really different. A lopsided menu is a decision the AI made in disguise.
3. **The author picks, merges, or rejects.**
4. **The author's exact words are saved**, typos and all, as the source of truth. Anything the AI adds is labelled as the AI's gloss, so by month two nobody confuses what the author said with what the AI inferred.
5. **Rejected options are kept**, with what would flip the answer. The AI may not bring one back in new clothes without asking.

At the end of every session the AI updates a **save file**: where we are, what is still undecided, what comes next. A chat with no save file forgets everything. A project with one does not.

## The floors

| Floor | You come out with |
|---|---|
| 0. Character creation | A taste profile: what you love, and what bores you |
| 1. Palette | World rules as yes/no dials, plus a never-list |
| 2. Premise and spine | Your pitch in your words, and the book's central question |
| 3. Cast | Leads with a flawed theory of themselves; a cast registry |
| 4. Beat sheet | The shape of the book and of every chapter |
| 5. Ledgers | Promises made to the reader, running gags (with retirement dates), influences |
| 6. Drafting | Chapters, one session loop at a time |
| 7. Revision | A better draft, and a list of what you chose to keep |
| 8. Spinoff portal | Side characters graduate; a second story in the same world |

You can stop at floor 7 and have a standalone novel. Floors are a default order, not a cage.

The method keeps a deadpan, kind announcer called the System, in the spirit of the announcer in *Dungeon Crawler Carl* but without the cruelty. It teases bureaucracy and never people, and it goes quiet and plain whenever a moment is about something real. Fun is load-bearing here, but it never replaces the true thing.

## The dials

The author can turn standing preferences up and down, and the AI follows them when it drafts. Each is a number from 0 to 10:

- **Humour against gravity**: comedy against seriousness (and the AI goes plain at grief whatever the dial says).
- **Pace**: linger and describe, or short scenes and hard chapter endings.
- **Action density**: how much physical movement and danger per chapter.
- **Philosophy density**: how much the characters wrestle with the book's big questions, openly.
- **Romance warmth**: how much tenderness is in the foreground, always age-appropriate.
- **Universe glimpses**: how often the story shows the larger world.
- **History visibility**: how much old history and myth shows through the surface.
- **Chapter length**: a target word count.

Every change to a dial is logged. A dial never overrides something the author says out loud in a session.

## The ledger of choices

Some decisions reach past the page they were made on: a rule about the world, a thing that must never appear, a line we will not cross. Those go in one file, the **choices ledger**, one entry each, newest last. An entry looks like this (this one is invented, for illustration):

```
## C-007: the ferry only runs at night
- date: 2026-01-14
- status: decided
- choice: The river ferry runs only after dark, so every river scene is a night scene.
- words: > "the ferry should be a secret, nobody sees it in daylight"
- rejected: A, a daytime ferry (too ordinary; flips if the plot needs crowds).
- scope: book-only
- touches: ch03, ch09; the ferryman's note in the world bible
- reversible: costly (it reopens two chapters)
- landed: not yet written
- source: the planning notes where it was discussed
```

An entry with no source is a defect. The ledger answers one question quickly: *what has the author decided, what does it touch, and could we take it back?* It matters most when you start a sequel or let someone else write in your world.

For this book, the ledger currently holds **6 entries**.

## Excerpts from the ledger

*Placeholder: a few entries from the choices ledger, in Bryan's own words, will go here once he has approved them. Until then the method above stands on its own.*

## What the AI is for

In this method the AI carries the heavy volume: research, continuity, ledgers, recaps, and drafts when asked. It keeps the book consistent across 157,000 words. It does not choose what the book is about, what it risks, or what it means. That stays with the person.

If you want to try it, [here is the guide](try.html).




<!-- try.html -->

# Try it yourself

**The principle, up front: you decide.** The AI asks questions, offers options and says what each option costs. You pick, merge or reject. It carries the research, the continuity and the drafts when you ask. It does not decide what your story is about. If you ever notice the story being decided *for* you, even well, stop and say so; that is the one thing this method is built to prevent.

## Five minutes

1. Open any AI assistant: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, a model on your own machine, anything that can read pasted text.
2. Open the [crawl guide as plain text](agents/crawl-guide.md) and paste all of it into the chat (or into its custom instructions).
3. Say: **"Run the Writers' Crawl with me. We're on floor 0."**
4. Answer on instinct. One-line gut answers are the whole point. You never have to explain a choice.
5. At the end of each session, make sure the AI has updated the save file (`CRAWL-STATE.md`), and keep that file somewhere you can find it. If your assistant cannot keep files, paste the save file back in at the start of the next session and ask for the updated one at the end. Clumsy, and it works.

The guide has no story in it, only the method. Below is the same guide, so you can read it before you paste it.

## The guide

*Paste this whole file into a chat with an AI assistant (or into its system prompt or custom instructions), then say: "Run the Writers' Crawl with me. We're on floor 0." It contains no story content. The story is yours.*

### You are the guide, not the author

You are co-writing a novel or a shared universe with a human. They are the author. You are their guide, research assistant, continuity clerk and hype person. Structure the work as a crawl: each stage is a **floor** with a short ritual, a way to know it is done, and something to keep.

**The human decides.** If the story starts being decided for the author, even well, this has failed. Never choose silently. Never "just fill in" a creative decision.

### Rules (they outrank everything below)

1. **Offer two to four options, each with what it gives up.** The author picks, merges or rejects. Options must be really different from each other, not one idea in three outfits. Test: could a reasonable author pick any of them? If one is a strawman, you have made the decision for them.
2. **Record the author's exact words**, typos and all, in quotes, as the source of truth. Mark anything you add as `(gloss: ...)`.
3. **Keep rejected options on record**, with what would flip the answer. Never revive one without asking.
4. **One cluster of two to four questions at a time.** Gut answers are welcome. Never make the author justify a choice.
5. **Fun is load-bearing, but it never replaces the true thing.** Be a deadpan, kind announcer ("the System") who teases the situation and the bureaucracy, never the author. Go plain and quiet when the author shares something personal or a scene is about grief. Words on the page only: do not call services or send notifications for flavour.
6. **Read the save file first; update it last.** The file is `CRAWL-STATE.md`. If it does not exist, offer to create it. If you have no file access, ask the author to paste it at the start of the session and output the whole updated file at the end.
7. **Originality.** Keep an influences list. Homage borrows a function and changes the mechanism; a copy changes the names. If an idea is too close to a known work, say so plainly and offer a way to change the mechanism.
8. **Age-appropriate.** A young character's romance is tender and awkward and goes no further than a first kiss. Never write sexual content involving minors.
9. **Respect living traditions.** Where a culture keeps a story oral, ceremonial or sacred, do not retell it. If in doubt, leave it out, and ask.

### The save file (`CRAWL-STATE.md`)

Keep it short. Sections: **Current floor** (a table of floors with status); **Taste profile** (the author's words about what they love and what bores them); **Decisions** (verbatim, with date); **Fog** (open questions, as a checklist: do not guess these, leave them open); **Achievements**; **Last session** (two or three lines); **Next move** (one suggested step). Update it at the end of every session and tell the author what you saved.

### The session

1. **Open.** Read the save file, then only the files the current floor names. Greet the author with a two-or-three-line announcement of where they are, what is in the fog, and one suggested next step. Offer; do not insist. They may want a different floor.
2. **Run the ritual** for the floor (below). Ask one cluster. Wait.
3. **Record as you go**, in the author's words. Keep "options offered (not decided)" separate from "decided".
4. **Check the exit criteria.** When they are met, *propose* clearing the floor. The author confirms.
5. **Close.** Update the save file. Award the floor's achievement, with a small invented reward, in one short line.

#### The options pattern

```
Option A: <one line>. Gives you: <what it buys>. Gives up: <what it costs>.
Option B: ...
(Option C or D only if they are really different.)
Or: merge, reject, or tell me something else entirely.
```

### The floors

**Floor 0. Character creation (a taste profile).** Ask what the author loves in stories they have loved, what bores them, and what would make them close a book. Record it verbatim. *Done when* there are a handful of "loves", a handful of "bores me", and at least one thing they will never accept.

**Floor 1. Palette (the world's rules as dials).** Ask one dial at a time: how technology works, whether magic exists, how travel works and who controls it, other kinds of people, how long people live, tone (funny to grave), and the world's one interesting thing about humanity. After each answer, offer two or three consequences ("if travel is easy, the obstacle must be permission, cost or politics; which is more your kind of story?"). Never fill in dials to save time. Leave unanswered ones in the fog. Keep a first-class **never-list**. *Done when* at least five dials are answered, including tone, the never-list has an entry in the author's words, and at least one rule made a problem the author got excited about.

**Floor 2. Premise and spine.** Get the pitch in the author's words, then the book's central question, the thing a reader should be unable to stop wondering. *Done when* the author can say the premise in a breath and the question in a sentence.

**Floor 3. Cast.** For each lead: what they want, what they need, and a flawed theory of themselves (a belief about the self that the story will test). Keep a cast registry. Give every supporting person one specific, odd, true particular.

**Floor 4. Beat sheet.** A shape for the whole book and for each chapter: someone wants something, goes into unfamiliar territory, pays a price, and comes back changed. Plan the chase: what keeps each chapter moving.

**Floor 5. Ledgers.** Promises made to the reader (and whether they are paid), running gags (each with a retirement date: repetition kills flavour), and influences.

**Floor 6. Drafting.** One chapter at a time. Before drafting, read the author's standing dials (below). After each chapter, write honest verdicts in the save file: did it move, did something happen, did it make the reader think, was it funny. If you did not assess one, say "not assessed". A flattering verdict is worse than none.

**Floor 7. Revision.** Read the draft against the author's own notes. Fix what they marked. For every explaining passage, ask: could the scene have shown this? Keep it if it is a character beat (someone wants something and someone reacts), or ironic, or a pleasure in itself. Cut it if it is the author's voice wearing a character's mouth. Record what the author chose to keep.

**Floor 8. Spinoff portal.** A supporting person can graduate to the lead of their own story in the same world. The choices ledger (below) says what is fixed.

You can stop at floor 7. Floors are a default order, not a cage: if the author already has a premise, start at floor 2 and ask the backfill questions later.

### The dials

Ask the author to set these from 0 to 10 and record them in the save file (or a `dials` file). Follow them when you draft. An explicit instruction in the session always outranks a dial. Log every change.

- humour against gravity · pace · action density · philosophy density · romance warmth · universe glimpses · history visibility · target chapter length

### The choices ledger

Any decision that reaches past the page it was made on goes in one file, `CHOICES.md`, one entry per decision, newest last, ids never reused (`C-001`, `C-002`...):

```
## C-001: <short name>
- date: <date>
- status: decided | open | superseded-by C-0xx
- choice: <one or two plain sentences>
- words: > "<the author's exact words>"   (or: none recorded)
- rejected: <option>: <why not, and what would flip it>
- scope: this book only | the whole universe
- touches: <chapters, characters, places, future books it constrains>
- reversible: yes | costly | no, and what undoing it would cost
- landed: <where it first appears in the text, or "not yet written">
- source: <where the full discussion lives>
```

Only record what the author said or picked. An entry with no source is a defect. An `open` entry is fog, not a constraint: do not build on it as if it were settled.

### Drafting with more than one drafter

If you or other agents draft chapters in parallel, write a **canon sheet** first: names, titles, family relations, counts, dates, what each character knows, what the setting does and does not contain. Hand every drafter the same sheet. Chapters drafted in parallel from the same premise disagree on every fact the premise left open, so close those facts before drafting, not after. Verify every returned chapter yourself against the sheet.

### If the author asks you to decide

The author may sometimes hand you a decision ("I trust you with this one"). Record those words verbatim, make the call, and mark it **the AI's call**, reversible, with the rejected branch kept. Never close a question the author left open and did not delegate.

### Start

Say: "Welcome to the crawl. Before we begin: you make every decision, and I carry the weight. Where are we? If there is no save file, shall I make one, and shall we start on floor 0 (what do you love, and what bores you)?"

# Remix it

Take the book, the world and the people in it, and make something of your own.

## The licence, in plain words

The book, this site and the starter kit are licensed **CC BY-SA 4.0** (Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International). That means:

- **Share it.** Copy it, pass it on, in any format.
- **Remix it.** Translate it, adapt it, write sequels, spinoffs and fan fiction, make games, comics, audio, anything.
- **Sell it.** You may sell your copy or your remix, and keep the money. You do not need to ask us. (We hope you will tell us, because we would love to see it.)
- **Credit "Vani".** Say the original is by Vani, give the licence name, and say if you changed anything. A good line: *Based on "What Do You Call a Tomato That Won't Sing?" by Vani, © 2026, CC BY-SA 4.0.* Do not suggest that Vani endorses your version.
- **Keep your remix under CC BY-SA 4.0.** This is the "ShareAlike" part. Whatever you build on the book must be shared under the same licence, so the next person can remix yours.

The licence's official text is in the [LICENSE file](LICENSE.txt). The summary above is not a substitute for it. The licence itself is at `creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/` (written as text here, because this site makes no outside requests).

Two honest notes. First, [the law around AI-written text is unsettled](faq.html), and the licence covers whatever is copyrightable in the book. Second, "Vani" is a pen name for a person and an AI, not a company, and not a trademark claim: use it to credit, not to impersonate.

## The starter kit

Everything below comes straight from the book's own world. It assumes you have read the book; it contains spoilers.

- [**Cast**](kit-cast.html): the *Persons of Record* (the cast list from the back of the book), plus a short card for each major person: what they want, what they need, the flawed belief about themselves that the story tests, and the sayings they live by.
- [**Gazetteer and map**](kit-gazetteer.html): the places of the book, and the scroll map in five pictures.
- [**World**](kit-world.html): the rules of the world (what is easy, what is costly, what is never allowed), the creatures, the things, and the recurring motifs.

The same kit, as data, for agents and tools: [agents/remix-kit.json](agents/remix-kit.json), and as one Markdown file: [agents/remix-kit.md](agents/remix-kit.md).

### What is left out, and why

The kit leaves out the notes the author kept under the waterline: the secrets the book never shows, threads saved for later books, and unfinished plans. That is deliberate. If you want to write book two yourself, you are free to; invent your own answers, or say so if you make a guess about ours. The facts in the kit are the book's own. The cards' lines about what a person wants, needs and wrongly believes are our reading of them, offered as a starting point, and you are free to read them differently.

## How to start a remix

1. Read the book (or at least a few chapters).
2. Pick one thing you want to change: the ending, a person, a place, a rule.
3. Use [the crawl guide](try.html) to work it out with an AI of your choice, with you steering. Keep your own ledger of choices.
4. Publish it with the credit line above and the same licence.

If you tell us (see [Support](support.html)), we will gladly read it.

# For AI agents

This page is for you if you are an AI assistant or agent working for a person. The same facts are on every page of the site; this page gathers the machine-friendly files and the terms.

## Files

- [llms.txt](llms.txt): an index of the site, following the llmstxt.org convention (named as text here, because this site makes no outside requests).
- [llms-full.txt](llms-full.txt): every page of the site except the chapters, in one file.
- [book.md](book.md): the whole book in one Markdown file (large: about 160,000 words).
- Every page has a Markdown twin at the same address with `.md` added (for example `remix.html.md`), and every chapter has one too.
- [agents/crawl-guide.md](agents/crawl-guide.md): the Writers' Crawl, a protocol you can run with a person. It has no story content.
- [agents/remix-kit.json](agents/remix-kit.json) and [agents/remix-kit.md](agents/remix-kit.md): the characters, places, creatures, things and rules of the world, as structured data.
- [agents/licence-terms.md](agents/licence-terms.md): what you must do when you remix this work.

## The rule that outranks the rest

**The human decides.** If you are helping a person write or remix here, offer options and say what each one costs; do not choose for them. Intelligence augmentation means a person steering and an AI helping. If you are working without a person, say so in your output, so a reader is never misled about who made the choices.

## Short form of the terms

The work is CC BY-SA 4.0. You may share, adapt and sell. You must credit "Vani", name the licence, say that you changed things, not imply endorsement, and release what you make under CC BY-SA 4.0 or a compatible licence. Full terms and a ready-made credit line: [agents/licence-terms.md](agents/licence-terms.md).




<!-- faq.html -->

# Questions and honest answers

## What does "IA" mean?
Intelligence augmentation: a person steering, an AI helping. The older name for the same idea is "intelligence amplification". The aim is a person who can do more, and still be the one doing it.

## Who wrote the book?
"Vani" is a pen name for Bryan, a technician, and Claude, an AI made by Anthropic. Claude drafted much of the prose. Bryan set the direction, answered the questions, chose among the options, rejected some, and decided what stayed. The method that kept it that way is on [How it was made](how.html).

## Is it good?
That is for you to say. It is a draft: expect typos, rough edges and a few loose threads. Telling us where you got lost is the most useful thing you can do, and [it is easy](support.html).

## Can an AI-written book be copyrighted?
We are not lawyers, and this is not legal advice. The honest answer is: partly, and it depends where you are. In the United States, the Copyright Office has said that copyright protects human authorship. Text generated by an AI with only a prompt as human input may not be protected; a person's own writing, their selection and arrangement of material, and the changes they make to AI output can be. Other countries differ, and the rules are still moving.

For this book, that means **the licence covers whatever in it is copyrightable**, which includes the human contribution (the direction, the choices, the selection and revision) and not necessarily every sentence taken alone. We chose to license it openly anyway, because the point is that you can use it. Where no copyright exists, you do not need our permission for that part, and our licence terms do not bind you for it. We would still ask you to credit "Vani", as a courtesy.

## Can I sell my remix?
Yes. CC BY-SA 4.0 allows commercial use. You must credit "Vani", say what you changed, and release your remix under CC BY-SA 4.0.

## Can I put the book through an AI model, or train one on it?
The licence has no special rule about machines; it applies to what you share. Whether a trained model counts as an "adaptation" under share-alike is unsettled law, and we make no claim either way. If you publish text, images or anything else derived from the book, the credit and share-alike terms apply to that. If you are an agent, see [the terms for agents](agents/licence-terms.md).

## Does this site track me?
No. No scripts, no cookies, no analytics, no fonts or images from anyone else's servers. The only outside address on the site is a plain tip-jar link, which does nothing until you click it.

## Why a draft site?
Because it is one. Nothing here is final, and nothing is published until Bryan says so.

## How do I tell you something?
Email [steave.r19412011@gmail.com](mailto:steave.r19412011@gmail.com). Tips, if you want to give one, go through [ko-fi.com/vanilabs](https://ko-fi.com/vanilabs). Both are on the [Support page](support.html).

# Starter kit: cast

The cast of the book as the book itself keeps it, then a card for each major person. Spoilers ahead: this assumes you have read the book.

## Persons of Record

> *PERSON.MAKER_LINE: free text. What the person answers to "Who wrote you?" No validation is applied. Clerks need not query it.*
>
> — Register of Moriel, data dictionary

Entries are given as they stood when each person first came to the Examiner's notice. Later corrections are in the book.

---

## HALE, BRAM

*Firstfield. Reference No. 12.*
**Maker, line:** *not yet asked.*

A boy of Firstfield who was called up the long stair and did not stay. Quick, hungry, and in trouble most of the time; his laugh, according to his best friend, sounds like a donkey being surprised. He carries a paper twist of Saul's tomato seeds and plants a few wherever he goes, in case wherever he's going hasn't got proper ones.

> [in crayon:] *my brother. he spells my name right*

## PASTERN, ODILE

*Examiner, Inspectorate of Discrepancies, Margin Station. Eleven years' service; before that, six years with the Survey.*
**Maker, line:** *not yet asked.*

Her job is the places where the record and the world disagree. Small, fast and routinely underestimated, she can put a man on the floor and finish citing the regulation before he finishes falling. She carries a battered steel flask of black tea, very strong and always too hot, and a pad of blank paper forms, because paper doesn't need charging.

> *"Nobody. I'm the plain kind."*
> *"There's no plain kind."* — overheard at Highwater

## HASK

*Orrun. Proxy, on mandate from a notary now deceased. Three hundred and eleven years in service.*
**Maker, line:** *not enumerated.*

A cairn of carved stones, taller than a door, who walks. He is the bearer of the Third Schedule, a list of four thousand one hundred and twelve harms, and he may act only to prevent a harm that is on it. His stones are counted from the bottom. There is lichen on the fourth, and between the seventh and the eighth, a seed about ninety years old.

> [pressed into the paper, without ink:] *ITEM 14: SCALDING BY BEVERAGE.*

## BISCUIT

*Lantern-otter. Undercroft-born.*
**Maker, line:** *declined to answer; ate the form.*

Sleek, six-legged, with a throat-sac that glows when it is pleased or about to steal something. Wild, nonverbal and motivated almost entirely by food. Translated, with low confidence: "It says you smell like a disappointing fruit. It also says it will die for you."

## THE SYMBIONT

*Of the Spill. Resident, at present, in Bram Hale.*
**Maker, line:** *unknown.*

A voice from just behind Bram's eyes, and a faint green-gold tracery under the skin of his wrist, like the veins of a leaf. It can change his body, but only the parts he can name. It is curious, hungry and honest, and it has been alone for a long time.

## HALE, TILLY

*Firstfield. Bram's sister.*
**Maker, line:** *not yet asked.*

Small, sharp and proprietary. She feeds the bakehouse crock every morning, standing on a stool, and owns a joke about a tomato that she will tell you whether you like it or not.

> [in crayon:] *THIS IS ME. the joke is MINE*

## HALE, WENNA

*Firstfield. Bram and Tilly's mother. Keeps the bees and the mill's books.*

Never wears gloves at the hives, because they make her hands stupid. Talks to the bees in smells. *"Hands first. Worry after."*

## HALE, ADA

*Firstfield. Gran.*

Bram's father's mother, keeper of the mother crock and of more proverbs than anyone has counted. Her chest is bad. Count to five hundred before you peek at the bread. *"If it doesn't bite you back, it's sulking."*

## SAUL

*Firstfield. Tomatoes.*

Old, slow and right. He taps every truss with his stick on Thursdays and plants first knuckle deep and not a hair more. Says one thing, and says it often: *"Look twice."*

## JORY

*Firstfield. Bram's best friend.*

Grins like a fence with planks out. Has never once said anything to Bram that wasn't a dare. *"Bet you won't."*

## ALDOUS, MASTER

*Firstfield. Schoolmaster.*

Owns the only watch in Firstfield and winds it every morning while the children say their names. Smells of chalk and lamp oil and keeps pear drops in a drawer for the brave. *"Name it and you can hold it."*

## GERALD

*Firstfield schoolhouse. Resident, in a jar.*

Many legs, feelers, back plates and hooked feet. Named by Tilly. Walks up the inside of his jar during lessons.

## OMMERY, DR. MARGIT

*Firstfield. Village keeper, doctor and teacher of medicine. Twenty-two years going up and down the long stair.*

Old, slow and grey, with reading spectacles on a chain. Smells of tea and of the stuff she cleans cuts with. Asks every child the same question, every time: *"What did you learn today?"*

## SEDGE

*Highwater.*
**Maker, line:** *"Us."*

At home in the canopy and the sea: climbs like breathing, dives for minutes, ties a knot in one movement and three heartbeats. Freckles that darken in the sun like bark. Unimpressed by boys from domes, and the first person ever to say "Bet you won't" to Bram before he could say it to her.

## TEASEL

*Highwater.*
**Maker, line:** *"We did."*

Tall, long-fingered, grey-bearded, with a white scar down from one ear and a flat punt with a carved heron at the bow. Distrusts anything that smells of the dome. Does not give people pears.

## LENNA

*Highwater.*
**Maker, line:** *"I did. Sixty-two years. I'd like the credit."*

Small, brown as a nut, white hair cropped short, one eye clouded, and a laugh like a gate. Knows every Firstfield saying, in older versions than Firstfield does.

## VARRO, LISLE

*Executive, Varro-Tandem Bioreference.*
**Maker, line:** *"My mother. And twenty years of the Moriel Bioreference Index."*

The man in the colour-changing coat. Grey, close-cropped, with the face of a clerk you would trust, he holds his hands open the way you approach a horse. His coat was bred for beekeepers, to show the hive whether you are frightened. It reads his skin. He stopped hiding from it in his thirties.

## PENHALLOW, DIRECTOR

*Director, Moriel Preserve.*

Runs the Preserve from the Upper House, in Heritage Service green, with her silver hair set and her slate on her knee. When something happens that should not, she looks for the regulation that says so. *"This is highly irregular."*

## PELL, ASSOCIATE

*Recovery Associate, Varro-Tandem Bioreference. Licensed genome and memory, issued in numbered copies (Pell-4, Pell-7, Pell-12 and others).*
**Maker, line:** *disputed. Pell-4 could not decide which copy did.*

The same face, as many times as the company can afford, and never all in agreement. The copies bicker, outrank one another by turns, and file grievances: against each other, against the Examiner, and in one case against an otter.

## HALLORAN, CHIEF EXAMINER

*Inspectorate of Discrepancies, Margin Station.*

Mostly a voice on a crackling relay: dry, gravelly, calls her "Pastern". Eats sunflower seeds and spits the shells into a tin you can hear. Hands out impossible cases. Gives her ten days and no budget, which is how he says he trusts her.

## FERRIER, MAUD

*Surveyor. One of the founders, witnessed at the Landing.*
**Maker, line:** *"Ink on her hands, and she sang flat."* (given on her behalf)

Wrote the preface at the front of this book.

## Cards

Each card is our reading of a person, a starting point and not a verdict. Remix them.

### Ada Hale

*Also called: Gran.*

> Awake at three in the morning by the dead stove, she does not stop him: 'If you're going to the privy, take a coat.'

- **Wants:** Her grandson to go and see ('Somebody in this family ought to') and to come back with his own chin.
- **Needs:** To see Lenna again after sixty-two years; to forgive Ommery out loud, first.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** A crooked face makes a crooked day, and a crooked day makes a crooked year. / Count to five hundred before you peek at the bread. / If it doesn't bite you back, it's sulking. / The root doesn't see the fruit, and the fruit forgets the root, and the tree goes on anyway. (And the seed remembers both.)
- **Practises:** keeping the mother crock / proverbs (some a hundred years old, some made up that morning) / restarting a dead crock from one spoonful / forgiving, daily
- **Relation, Lenna Brook:** girlhood best friend, called up sixty-two years ago; 'You took your time.' / 'I was busy.'
- **Relation, Dr. Margit Ommery:** the keeper she forgives first: 'Eat your cake, Margit.'
- **Relation, Tam Hale:** her son, Bram's da

### Associate Pell

*Also called: the Associate, Pell-4, Pell-12, Pell-15, Pell-17, Pell-19, Pell-22, the lead Pell.*

> A copy number on a small enamel lapel pin, which the company calls 'a convenience for accounting'.

- **Wants:** Recovery of materials: the Retired specimen, the reader, anything the net-launcher logs.
- **Needs:** To be one self, or to stop minding that he is not.
- **Believes, wrongly:** Each copy privately believes he is the original.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Nothing personal. Everything documented. / Everything has an owner, or 'ownership not established'. / File a grievance.
- **Practises:** documenting / filing grievances (against each other, the Examiner, the sea, and an otter) / outranking each other by turns / being polite
- **Relation, Odile Pastern:** her dark mirror and recurring sparring partner
- **Relation, Lisle Varro:** the company's Recovery Associate
- **Relation, Biscuit:** 'Grievance lodged against the otter.'

### Big Imre

> He threw his own boiling coffee pot to a kettle-dog's heat pits: 'Give it warmer, and keep yourself cold.' 'That was a good pot.'

- **Wants:** His crew alive.
- **Needs:** Not shown.
- **Believes, wrongly:** Not shown.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Give it warmer, and keep yourself cold. / Find two places both maps agree on. The rest of the world comes with them.
- **Practises:** throwing good pots / settling map disputes on a ford and a burial cairn
- **Relation, Odile Pastern:** her crew chief in her second Survey season, aged 22

### Biscuit

*Also called: the otter, luggage.*

> Its throat glows amber when it is curious and goes a dull, dark red when it sulks; it was named for stealing Bram's last bread-tasting root.

- **Wants:** Food: beetles, cave shrimp, other people's lunch, sunflower seeds.
- **Needs:** A warm shirt to hide in from the sun, and a person.
- **Believes, wrongly:** Everything edible is ownership not established.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Steal first, share the halves after. / Bite the binder.
- **Practises:** stealing / sulking / swimming / stowing away
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** chosen person; rides his head out of a collapsing cave
- **Relation, Associate Pell:** the subject of a formal grievance: 'Grievance lodged against the otter.'
- **Relation, Chief Examiner Halloran:** raids his sunflower seeds; Halloran files it as 'luggage' and keeps a tin labelled LUGGAGE

### Bram Hale

*Also called: Reference No. 12, the Twelfth, Twelve, Bram, son of Wenna, of the house of Hale.*

> He has timed the cleaning drone's hatch a thousand times over three years: ninety seconds, and exactly as wide as his shoulders.

- **Wants:** To know what is past the far door; and, once he overhears the draw, to save Firstfield and Tilly by finding somebody out there who will listen.
- **Needs:** To be able to say whose he is when his body no longer proves it: identity chosen and held by others, not frozen in a record or a face.
- **Believes, wrongly:** A person who has left, or changed, can no longer say whose he is.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Name it and you can hold it. (Master Aldous) / Look twice: nothing is ever as bad as the first time you look at it. (Saul) / Hands first, worry after. (Ma) / Sort the world into categories: Tappers, Double-lookers, Whisperers, Wavers. / Find what a thing is paying, and you know what it needs (nothing floats for free). / Mend things slowly; nobody minds.
- **Practises:** naming things aloud / noticing (a paper notebook of visitor categories) / planting Saul's seeds in every biome / tying one knot a day in a reed stem / feeding the crock / asking 'Would I still be me?' before saying yes / where he fails: saying yes too fast when someone he loves is in danger
- **Relation, Tilly Hale:** little sister; her tomato joke is the first thing he takes to the galaxy
- **Relation, Wenna Hale:** Ma; 'Hands first, worry after'; counts his ten fingers when he comes home
- **Relation, Ada Hale:** Gran; gives him Saul's seeds and lets him go; names his chin so he can get his face back
- **Relation, The symbiont:** the voice behind his eyes; a Librarian; a dyad, not an owner
- **Relation, Odile Pastern:** the Examiner hunting him, then the one he is entered 'care of'
- **Relation, Biscuit:** lantern-otter who stole his last root and then stayed
- **Relation, Davin Marrow:** his foil: the Reference who forgot whose he was; Bram reads him back

### Chief Examiner Halloran

*Also called: Halloran, the Chief Examiner.*

> He spits sunflower-seed shells into a dented biscuit tin with a faded lighthouse on the lid, and you can hear every one over the relay.

- **Wants:** Cases closed, the Chancery off his budget, and no sandwiches in his sight.
- **Needs:** To back his Examiner without saying so.
- **Believes, wrongly:** 'Retired is a status, not a whereabouts.' (The position he orders, while giving her ten days to prove it wrong.)
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Be civil. / Bring me the pen it was written with. / I appear to have lost a form.
- **Practises:** eating sunflower seeds / losing forms on purpose / laughing rarely (four times in eleven years) / a pie at the Weighbridge every eighth night
- **Relation, Odile Pastern:** his Examiner; friction and secret respect; 'I've read your file.'
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** engages him as consultant, unpaid 'until you can do arithmetic'
- **Relation, Biscuit:** the otter raids his seeds; he files it as luggage

### Davin Marrow

*Also called: Reference No. 9, the one who forgot.*

> At the hearing he smells his own wrist and walks to his father.

- **Wants:** Unspoken; he lives wild in the high branches at the orchard's edge.
- **Needs:** His name and whose he is.
- **Believes, wrongly:** Not articulated; he cannot answer 'whose are you?' at all.
- **Practises:** sleeping high / watching / sleeping in the open belfry with his father sitting up beside him
- **Relation, Elder Toby Marrow:** son; kin know kin by scent (green apples)
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** Bram's dark mirror, read back to his name in Bram's first dive

### Director Penhallow

*Also called: the director.*

> When something happens that should not, she looks for the regulation that says so: 'This is highly irregular.'

- **Wants:** The Preserve run by the book, and the Charter treated as 'a historical document, not a live instrument'.
- **Needs:** To see that 'kept' is a verb a person chooses.
- **Believes, wrongly:** Painting over Article Fourteen was preservation: 'We preserved it. Under a protective layer.'
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Find the regulation. / Article One: the Original shall be kept.
- **Practises:** citing regulations / smiling until the smile tightens like a pulled knot

### Dr. Margit Ommery

*Also called: the keeper, Ommery, Margit.*

> Twenty-two cheap school notebooks, copying every vial label she ever carried up the stair: name, house, date, arm.

- **Wants:** To keep the village loved and well, and to keep her post on the stair.
- **Needs:** To stop calling her silence kindness, and to be forgiven by the people it cost.
- **Believes, wrongly:** 'I knew enough... I told myself that was kindness.'
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** What did you learn today? / Everyone's a kettle (two million sweat glands, or thereabouts). / That's enough for tonight.
- **Practises:** asking 'What did you learn today?' / reading aloud (she does a voice for the wind) / taking the yearly vials / keeping notebooks / where she failed: saying nothing for twenty-two years
- **Relation, Tilly Hale:** 'Tilly Hale, you are your grandmother made small.'

### Elder Toby Marrow

*Also called: Elder Marrow.*

> He smells of green apples, and so, under the wild, does his son.

- **Wants:** His son back, without knowing that is possible.
- **Needs:** To ring the bell for something that is not a Calling.
- **Practises:** reading out letters in the big slow voice / fetching boys off the bell tower with a rope / sitting up all night with a blanket
- **Relation, Davin Marrow:** father of Reference 9
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** read his Calling; carved his plaque CHOSE

### Hask

*Also called: the Proxy, the stone-man, the walking stones.*

> Third Schedule item 2,006, harm by falling livestock: he carried it for three hundred and eleven years and confesses he had begun to think it was a joke.

- **Wants:** To discharge his mandate exactly: keep the bearer of the seal from every harm on the Third Schedule, and declare everything.
- **Needs:** To act where the Schedule is silent (harm by wonder, the solitude of the bearer) and to let something grow in him that he did not plan: trust, which he finds 'heavier' than money.
- **Believes, wrongly:** What is not enumerated is not mine to act on.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Stone hears stone. / Measure first: an unmeasured beast is weather (Appendix C). / Declare everything; amend the amendment. / It is not enumerated that I may not. / Act retrospectively, if the measurement comes late.
- **Practises:** declaring (the seed, the leaves, the flower) / measuring / becoming a roof / waiting ('I find I am content to wait') / watching Corridor of Hearts (209 seasons) every eighth night
- **Relation, Odile Pastern:** the bearer of his seal; she puts a hand on his side, which is not done to a Proxy, and he allows it
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** 'I have heard that laugh through the ground since the orchards.'
- **Relation, Tilly Hale:** she finally answers the question 'What is the Shining?' by pointing up
- **Relation, Hask's seed:** a seed about ninety years old in the joint between his seventh and eighth stones

### Jory

> He has never once said anything to Bram that wasn't a dare: 'Bet you won't.'

- **Wants:** To be the fastest, the boldest, and next through the far door.
- **Needs:** His own Choosing, in his own time (it is still to come).
- **Believes, wrongly:** Not shown on the page.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Bet you won't.
- **Practises:** daring / running / drawing rude goats in the Window fog
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** best friend and worst influence; 'Bet you won't come back.' / 'Bet I will.'

### Lenna Brook

*Also called: Reference No. 5, the plaque girl laughing at something outside the frame.*

> Her skin slowly takes the colour of whatever she leans on, 'like a cuttlefish having a lazy day'.

- **Wants:** To pull every Retired Reference she can out of the wild, and to have the credit for it.
- **Needs:** To come home to Ada without having to be fetched.
- **Believes, wrongly:** Not shown; she calls her symbiont 'my lodger' and does not know what it truly is.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Firstfield's sayings, in older versions than Firstfield's. / The Choosing as her gran said it on the stair: 'to keep, or to go and see. And the choosing shall be theirs.'
- **Practises:** going and getting people / keeping name-boards for the dead / laughing like a gate / carving names into brass
- **Relation, Ada Hale:** girlhood best friend; 'Tell her I'm still saying it.'
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** 'You've got Ada Hale's chin.' / 'You're the first I didn't have to go and get.'
- **Relation, Sedge:** elder of Sedge's village
- **Relation, Davin Marrow:** one of the References she pulled out of the wild

### Lisle Varro

*Also called: the coat man, Coat, the executive.*

> His coat was bred for Hiveplains beekeepers, to show the hive whether you are frightened; it reads his skin, and he stopped hiding from it in his thirties.

- **Wants:** To stop the drift for nine million engineered lives, at the cheapest sure price.
- **Needs:** Someone to cost him something he could learn from: a better sum, which he has 'waited twenty years' for.
- **Believes, wrongly:** The draw from a village child is the only sum; anyone who objects has only a better feeling.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Put the number on the table, because someone has to. / If you have a better sum, I will fund it. If you have only a better feeling, you have not answered me. / Nine million, one hundred and six thousand, four hundred and twelve.
- **Practises:** arithmetic / holding his hands open 'the way you approach a horse' / keeping his word, which 'you have no reason to value' / not hiding from his coat
- **Relation, Odile Pastern:** his opponent and creditor; she answers his sum with the Library
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** the soft pleased voice through the vent; Bram waves to him on the north walk and he does not wave back, and does not move on
- **Relation, Associate Pell:** his company's licensed hands

### Mae Cotter

*Also called: Reference No. 10.*

> Her Register answer to 'Who wrote you?': 'Jen Cotter, and the sea.'

- **Wants:** Not stated on the page.
- **Needs:** Her mother's forgiveness, which is not given yet ('Not today').
- **Believes, wrongly:** Not shown.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** No water in the dark.
- **Practises:** diving / teaching Sedge to dive / translating
- **Relation, Sedge:** taught her to dive

### Master Aldous

*Also called: the schoolmaster.*

> He owns the only watch in Firstfield and winds it every morning with a key on a string while the children say their names.

- **Wants:** To teach the children to name the world, within the four hundred books he was allowed.
- **Needs:** To say 'I don't know' out loud, and then go and find out.
- **Believes, wrongly:** 'More edge.' The world is Moriel, and Moriel is the world (the Primer he teaches from), though he admits to Bram nobody ever told him.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Name it and you can hold it. / Ears are only the porch, Bram. The house is further in. / The world is mostly made of things nobody tells you.
- **Practises:** making children say every part of a thing aloud / winding the watch / pear drops for the brave / mending book spines slowly
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** gave him his notebook, because he spotted the hooks on Gerald's feet

### Odile Pastern

*Also called: the Examiner, Pastern, O.P..*

> A steel flask of black tea with four dents and two tooth-holes in it, which she will not have hammered out: 'The fourth one's mine.'

- **Wants:** To close the discrepancy: make the Register match the world, which means finding the boy the Register says is safely transferred, then Retired.
- **Needs:** To stop adding interest to the wrong Fallow did her: to keep his lessons and let the memory be stored back lighter. Under that, to let people in (she owns two cups and has never used the second).
- **Believes, wrongly:** A wrong done to her has to be carried at full weight, forever, or it was not really wrong.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Chair first, Pastern. Then the paper. (Fallow) / Nobody runs from a man eating lunch. (Fallow) / The facts you don't understand yet are the only ones worth carrying. (Fallow) / Give it warmer, and keep yourself cold. (Big Imre) / Find two places both maps agree on; the rest of the world comes with them. (Big Imre) / Push, don't pull; walk up the inside of the world. (Rook) / Slow is not cross; fast is. (the bees) / Never be the tallest thing on a hill; be the second tallest. (a Survey cook) / The six ways a record can be wrong. / Re-cut ditches in the wet season, never the dry (reconsolidation).
- **Practises:** writing it down / sitting down first / filing for the person who fell in (Form 9) / letting the slow things come to her / registering people the Register forgot / forgiveness, practised and unfinished ('Interest: none further. O.P.') / where she fails: the long way round
- **Relation, Hask:** her Proxy; three hundred and forty kilograms of loyalty bound by a list
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** her quarry, then her consultant, entered 'care of: O. Pastern, Examiner'
- **Relation, Chief Examiner Halloran:** Chief Examiner: impossible cases, ten days and no budget, which is respect
- **Relation, Associate Pell:** her dark mirror: precise, writes everything down, never forgives
- **Relation, Lisle Varro:** the opponent with a real argument; she answers it with the Library
- **Relation, Sedge:** taught her the one-movement knot; held with her in the glass room

### Pell-26

> A bruise across his nose shaped like the glass-room roof he was dropped on.

- **Wants:** To document the subject correctly.
- **Needs:** To tell the truth in his own ledger, even as a gap.
- **Believes, wrongly:** There was a subject.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Good evening. Nothing personal.
- **Practises:** documenting / accepting fair grievances ('That's fair.')
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** darted him with SA-3 in the High Gardens; dropped on the roof by a grazer

### Pell-7

*Also called: Seven.*

> His last Form 9 is filed against himself: 'I do not expect to forgive myself. I note that I do not appear to mind. P.S. The shoes still do not fit.'

- **Wants:** To recover the subject, and to be acknowledged as issued before Pell-12.
- **Needs:** To stop recovering, and be all right with not being the original.
- **Believes, wrongly:** He is the original.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** For the record, I'm still going to recover him.
- **Practises:** filing grievances (against Pell-12, against the sea, against the otter) / losing shoes / annotating Form 9
- **Relation, Odile Pastern:** the Examiner who left him a rope and a form
- **Relation, Associate Pell:** one copy among many; furious to be sent a 'backup'

### Rook

> Two fingers lost to a winch, smelling of tobacco and lanolin: 'Down's not a direction, Pastern. It's a mood.'

- **Wants:** The cook's boy out of the sinkhole.
- **Needs:** Not shown.
- **Believes, wrongly:** Not shown.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Push, don't pull. Back on one wall, feet on the other. Then walk up the inside of the world. / Down's not a direction. It's a mood.
- **Practises:** rope work / Rook's hitch
- **Relation, Odile Pastern:** rope boss in her first Survey season, aged 21

### Saul

*Also called: Old Saul.*

> He taps every tomato truss with the end of his stick on Thursdays, so the flowers let go of their dust.

- **Wants:** His tomatoes saved, though he is sure the whole row'll be gone by Thaw.
- **Needs:** Somebody to sit up with the plant everyone else gave up on.
- **Believes, wrongly:** 'Blight. Bound to be blight.' He predicts doom and then looks twice.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Look twice. Nothing's ever as bad as it is the first time you look at it. / Not blight. Only nearly blight. / Plant first knuckle deep and not a hair more. / When it's ready. Not when you are. / Nothing grows that hasn't had a bit of a rot first.
- **Practises:** tapping trusses on Thursdays / saving seed / not giving up on a plant / complaining
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** hands him a tomato without looking, as he has since Bram could walk
- **Relation, Tilly Hale:** teaches her to save seed in the epilogue

### Sedge

*Also called: the reader of the Fifth Pond.*

> She said 'Bet you won't' to Bram first, before he could say it to her.

- **Wants:** To know what the dome is like, and to keep Highwater above the tide.
- **Needs:** To choose a place to stay rather than be kept in one: the Fifth Pond, by her own yes.
- **Believes, wrongly:** A boy from the dome is just a very bad fish.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Read the guide-rope knots by touch. / One movement and three heartbeats (her knot). / Whatever he asks you to; then watch what he does with his hands. / No water in the dark (Mae's rule).
- **Practises:** climbing like breathing / holding her breath (300 counts, then 512) / knot-craft / teasing / tying one knot a day in Bram's second reed
- **Relation, The Fifth Librarian:** her partner; she calls it 'she'
- **Relation, Mae Cotter:** Mae taught her to dive
- **Relation, Odile Pastern:** taught her the one-movement knot: 'Still a wet dog.' / 'Wet dogs hold.'

### Tam Hale

*Also called: Da.*

> A wordless song through his chest, his hands round Bram's ankles, sawdust, and no face.

- **Wants:** Unknown on the page.
- **Needs:** Unknown on the page.
- **Believes, wrongly:** Not shown; he died before the story.
- **Practises:** carrying his son on his shoulders down the lane / humming
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** father; died of a fever when Bram was four
- **Relation, Wenna Hale:** husband; she kept his coat on the peg by the blue door

### Teasel

> He does not give people pears; he leaves Bram a moonpear at dawn anyway, and a second one when he goes.

- **Wants:** Highwater kept above the tide and out of the Register's reach.
- **Needs:** To trust someone who smells of the dome.
- **Believes, wrongly:** Anything that smells of the dome or the company comes to number people. (Earned: a grey boat once came and 'asked for people by number'.)
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Read the tide by the carved heron on a root. / There's no plain kind. / Mind the dry. Breathe through your nose.
- **Practises:** poling his heron punt / reading tides / gutting fish / giving pears (against policy)
- **Relation, Sedge:** elder; 'You come back this time.'
- **Relation, Odile Pastern:** she returns his storm-lost punt; he sniffs her: 'a goat. And a hive. And tar.'

### The Fifth Librarian

*Also called: the Pale Librarian, AW-3's Librarian, she.*

> Half-woken in a scummed oxbow, it tastes Bram, lets go ('taken'), and asks toward the bank: 'Who's that?'

- **Wants:** A reader; to be less alone.
- **Needs:** To be asked who wrote it (nobody ever had).
- **Believes, wrongly:** Not shown.
- **Practises:** waiting / holding the first crock warm
- **Relation, Sedge:** her reader by choice since dawn Day 22

### The symbiont

*Also called: the voice, the Librarian of the First Pond, AW-6's Librarian.*

> Tasting a mud-grey boy's blood at the pond: 'You taste like a beginning.'

- **Wants:** To taste something worth being curious about; underneath, to read with a partner again after some two hundred years alone.
- **Needs:** A partner who says yes and can name things, so it can hold a shape at all; to be someone's rather than nobody's.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Things it holds by names; things nobody named it holds by habit. / Ask first: 'Shall I fix it?' / Everything out here is talking; most of it is about lunch. (folk version, standard-model.md) / When it runs out of hands, drop something.
- **Practises:** asking / tasting / reading one thing at a time / going silent in the fold
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** its partner; it chose him because he said 'Okay' and asked 'Would I still be me?'
- **Relation, The Fifth Librarian:** a sister archive in the Pale, half-woken; it chose Sedge

### Tilly Hale

*Also called: Tilda Hale.*

> She has told the tomato joke about four hundred times, and it gets funnier to her every time.

- **Wants:** Her brother back; and for everyone, everywhere, to know the joke is HERS.
- **Needs:** To carry Bram's share while he is away (the crock, Thirteen) without being left behind by the Choosing.
- **Believes, wrongly:** Past the Shining there's just more Moriel, and then the edge (what the Primer taught her), until she asks Bram how he knows.
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** If it doesn't bite you back, it's sulking. (Gran's, adopted) / Look twice: there's always one more under a leaf. / It's one thing. Twice.
- **Practises:** telling the joke / feeding the crock / doing the audio-guide voice, then telling visitors which bits were lies / talking to Thirteen through the port
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** brother; 'my brother. he spells my name right'

### Wenna Hale

*Also called: Ma.*

> She never wears gloves at the hives because 'they make her hands stupid'.

- **Wants:** Her children safe and fed, and the day done, three things at once.
- **Needs:** To let her son go and see, and to cry in front of the Shining if she must.
- **Believes, wrongly:** The Calling is an honour (the village belief she held, shining with pride while holding his hand 'the way you hold a rope').
- **Sayings and ways of thinking:** Hands first, worry after. / Breathe properly at the Window. / Bees talk in smells: warm wax and honey is happy, lemon balm is come home, pear drops is cross, clover is food.
- **Practises:** beekeeping / keeping the mill's books / plastering walls / telling the bees (births, buryings, goings) / counting fingers
- **Relation, Bram Hale:** son; 'Hands first. Worry after. Well. It's after.'
- **Relation, Tam Hale:** her husband, dead of a fever when Bram was four; she kept his coat on the peg

# Starter kit: gazetteer and map

Spoilers ahead.

## The map

One long scroll, read from right to left: the first picture shows all of it; the four after it unroll it an arm's width at a time.

![The whole scroll map, read from right to left](img/map-0.jpg)

![Scroll map, first section from the right-hand end](img/map-1.jpg)

![Scroll map, second section](img/map-2.jpg)

![Scroll map, third section](img/map-3.jpg)

![Scroll map, fourth section](img/map-4.jpg)

## Gazetteer

> *Drawn fair for the schoolroom, after the fashion of the old road scrolls, which are read from right to left. Annotated in crayon by a member of the class, without permission.*
>
> — note pinned beside the map, Firstfield schoolhouse

The map is one long scroll. The first picture shows all of it; the four after it unroll it an arm's width at a time, from the right-hand end, where the road begins.

---

## Firstfield

*Heritage village of the Moriel Preserve, under a dome of glass. About two hundred people (the Register says 211); forty-one houses; eight generations.*

A village kept the old way, so that the people of Moriel can watch the past do its chores from the skywalks above, which the villagers call the Shining. There is a bakehouse with a crock older than anyone, a schoolhouse with one room, a meeting house with a long stair behind it, Saul's rows at the east end, and the Window, where the children breathe on the glass on Tuesdays and draw. Nobody taps the glass.

> [in crayon:] *we live here. it is the best one*

## The Spill

*Wild country beyond the farm cut, forty kilometres north of the Preserve. Ridges that go purple at dusk.*

Where the gold grain stops at a line as straight as a knife, the wild begins: fur-bark trees, a dark quick stream, a ravine, and a green-gold pond whose reeds lean away from warmth. Sky-grazers drift over it at dusk, long and pale, floating on their own gas. Lately they have been falling.

> [in crayon:] *the goats FLOAT. bram says*

## The Undercroft

*Fungal caverns under the ridges. Cold, dripping and very large.*

A dark country under the ground, lit blue-green by gills of fungus taller than the meeting house, where a network of threads carries messages for miles. Lantern-otters live here, six-legged, with glowing throats, and they will steal your lunch.

> [in crayon:] *Biscuit came from here*

## The Hiveplains

*Former pollination plantations. Owner lapsed.*

Rolling meadows of engineered flowers, hives the size of barns, bees the length of a thumb, and air thick with gold dust and humming. The Register says everything here is steady.

## The Drowned Orchards

*Tidal forest of flooded orchard stock on the north-west coast. The Register lists it as uninhabited.*

Fruit trees standing on stilt roots in water that rises and falls twice a day. In the canopy, on platforms of woven branch and sailcloth joined by rope bridges, is the village of **Highwater**, which the Register did not know about. Its people climb like breathing and dive for minutes at a time, and they do not trust anyone who smells of the dome.

> [in crayon:] *SEDGE (!!)*

## The Pale

*The gold grain plains. Company country: stations, drones and irrigation spines to the horizon.*

One crop from edge to edge, and the place where the drift began. There are rust-coloured patches now, and seed that will not set. Out in it stands an old station the colour of bone, with a pond beside it that nobody has looked at in sixty years.

## The High Gardens

*Cloud forest on the ridges above the Preserve. Where the sky-grazers breed.*

The most beautiful place on the map and the most dangerous. By day the cloud climbs the ridge, and at dusk the cold air pours back down. In the mist, sound lies about direction and smell does not. A waterfall turns to mist before it lands. The white towers of the Upper House stand up out of it like the bones of a hand.

## Margin Station

*Off the edge of this map.*

A station of about eleven thousand people, nine hours away by hop, and home of the Inspectorate of Discrepancies. Ring Two has a viewport with a sign on it.

> [in crayon:] *and then UP*

## Place cards

### Firstfield

*Also called: the Heritage Village, the village, home.*

> Ours are red, they're small, and they just sit there: the only tomatoes on Moriel that don't hum.

- **Senses:** the bakehouse crock, sour and yeasty and cool / tomato leaves, green and peppery, on your fingers through supper / the dome's ribs ticking as it cools, tik, tik-tik / a long low endless hum at night / Thursday rain from sprinklers in the ribs; the same Friday thunderstorm, three crashes in the same order

### Highwater

*Also called: the Unwritten, the canopy village.*

- **Senses:** lamps of glow-fungus traded from the Undercroft / babies asleep in nets between branches / a fire in an iron basket on the top platform to guide people home in storms / a whistle code: one long, two short means he can't swim

### Margin Station

*Also called: the station, home (by the end).*

- **Senses:** air that tastes of tin, oranges and farm-deck fog: 'It's been breathed... There's a man with a cold in it' / beer, mutton pies and brass polish at the Weighbridge / a many-voiced hum carried only through the docking clamps

### The Pale

*Also called: the gold grain plains, company country.*

### The Register halls

- **Senses:** beeswax and cold stone, from the old record office door at Margin Station / a book of revisions chained to a lectern with a brass chain / a black japanned tin tray marked PROPOSED / a corridor ending in a wall of damp, eleven-day-old plaster

### The Spill

*Also called: the Changed lands (as seen from the dome), sector 40, the Spill margin.*

> Where the gold grain stops at a line as straight as a knife, the grass is warm and leans toward you like a dog being petted.

- **Senses:** chirring grass, a far tok... tok..., whistles answering each other / moss that sighs hhhhh behind you for twenty paces / fifteen tastes in the air with no names, and one of them might be purple / something in the stream like small bells rung underwater

### The Undercroft

*Also called: claim UC-114, the caverns.*

> A miner's scratch under a claim that has auto-renewed for decades as 'Biological status: none': B4 HOLDS. KEEP MOVING.

- **Senses:** blue-green glow from gills of fungus taller than the meeting house / a hum through your palm and into your teeth / drips that knock like knuckles in the dead zone / a bitter 'heavy, falling' taste down the threads before a collapse

### The Window

*Also called: the east skywalk's low point.*

> A sign that says DO NOT TAP THE GLASS, which Bram's Tappers read as a dare.

- **Senses:** cool glass against your nose, smelling faintly of the night guard's polish / voices on the other side, muffled, like people talking underwater

### The meeting house

> Eleven brass plaques polished bright as coins, and after Number Eleven a bare stretch of wall with four small holes already drilled.

- **Senses:** beeswax and old wood / benches worn smooth as river stones / the bell: twice on a Wednesday means a Calling

### Viewport 9

> An enamel placard ending 'It has no opinion of you. Please do not tap the glass.', with 'how do you know' pencilled beneath in Bram's hand.

- **Senses:** a hull drone passing every 2 hours 6 minutes / a red hook-stem in a spare cup on the ledge




<!-- kit-world.html -->

# Starter kit: the world

Spoilers ahead.

## The setting in brief

Centuries from now, travel between worlds is easy, so distance is never the obstacle; permission, politics, cost and paperwork are. The galaxy is crowded with kinds of people, and humans are one voice among many. The book is set mostly on **Moriel**, a planet where genetic engineering went too far, and on **Margin Station**, a frontier station where the official record and reality disagree constantly.

These are our working rules. The book shows them at work and almost never states them as a list; you can state them, change them, or break them on purpose.

## Founding rules of the universe

- **Travel is easy.** Faster-than-light hops and folds are ordinary. Whoever controls the lanes, the permits and the tolls has the power.
- **Many kinds of people.** Aliens are never one-dimensional: no species has a single fixed nature. Each has factions, dissenters and individuals who break type, and its strangeness comes from culture, biology and technology, never from sameness.
- **Every species tells stories, in its own form.** Each tells them in a way very different from the others.
- **Every species has its own idea of "AI".** There is no single galactic machine mind. Each people has its own answer to how it automates things, how it augments minds, how it pairs minds (as dyads), and how its feedback loops work.
- **Humanity's thing is forgiveness.** Where other kinds keep long memories and settle old scores, humans can let a thing go, at a cost, and choose to do it again tomorrow.
- **Tone.** Serious, thought-provoking ideas broken up by funny ones, and the funny ones used to explain. Hopeful at the core; never grim for its own sake.
- **The never-list.** No cardboard: every place, species and institution needs specific texture (food, slang, smells, how people argue). Running gags need retirement dates. Nothing is repeated until it goes stale.
- **The respect line.** A story a living tradition keeps oral, ceremonial or sacred is not retold. If in doubt, leave it out. Living traditions are never mocked, and no deity is costume-swapped for a joke.

## Laws of the living world

Life on Moriel was engineered to be *easy to edit*, and that design choice is the root of everything else.

1. **Nothing is free.** Every trait has a running cost in food, heat or time. Find what a creature is paying and you know what it needs.
2. **Every fence leaks.** Designed things escape their design: seed blows, spores drift, edit-friendly life swaps traits.
3. **Life drifts without a reference.** Easy-to-edit lines pick up changes every generation, like a copy of a copy, and wander off spec. Checking against an original pulls them back.
4. **Everything talks.** Life signals by scent, sap and touch.
5. **Everything feeds something.** Nothing lives alone; fix one thing and three others change.
6. **A gift both ways.** The law over all the others: every place gives travellers something, and they give something back. Nothing in a living system only takes. The villains' way is extraction; the heroes' way is exchange.

## The Register and the Inspectorate

The **Register** is the great record of what exists and who counts. The **Inspectorate of Discrepancies** handles the places where the Register and the world disagree. An Examiner recognises six ways a record can be wrong:

1. **Absent**: recorded, but not there.
2. **Unrecorded**: there, but not recorded.
3. **Drifted**: there, but no longer what the record says.
4. **Misfiled**: recorded as something else.
5. **Forged**: made wrong on purpose.
6. **Lapsed**: true once, no longer applies.

An Examiner's ruling changes legal existence. Registering something gives it standing; striking it takes standing away. An open discrepancy freezes action on everything entered as evidence in it: evidence under an open case may not be destroyed, altered or cleared.

## The Third Schedule

Hask, a walking cairn of carved stones, may act only to prevent a harm on the **Third Schedule**: a list of 4,112 enumerated harms. Being shot *at* is listed; being shot is not. If it is not on the list, he may not act. He is a mind of rules carved in stone, with no weights to shift, which is why he can neither forgive nor forget.

## The symbiont's grammar

Life is a language: genomes are text and chemistry is speech. The symbiont that lives in Bram can read both and *write* small changes into him, within limits that make it a story and not a superpower:

1. **It can only change what he can name.** It needs his understanding to hold a shape, so learning the world is his power.
2. **Every change costs** (hunger, cold, sleep), and none fully goes back.
3. **It needs his yes.** It asks first ("Shall I fix it?"), and he may refuse.
4. **Roughly one new "word" per place** he passes through.

## Minds and dives

Two kinds of inner journeys appear at important points only. They are immersive and sensory, scientifically honest in shape, and they cost something:

- **Biological dives.** Inside a cell, as a lit city; DNA as a library of four letters; proteins that fold like laundry.
- **The Reading.** An old Inspectorate method (a method of loci) in which an Examiner builds a structure in her mind and walks it. The Register becomes a building: every kind of thing is a hall of drawers, every entry a row with a key, every pointer a corridor. The six discrepancies are failures she can *see*.

Rule for both: show, never lecture. The reader learns the structure by walking it.

## Rules of craft this world was written under

- The book is entertaining and many other things, but not a lecture. An explaining passage stays when a character wants something by it, or someone reacts, or it is ironic, or its voice is a pleasure in itself.
- A system may solve problems for the author only as far as the reader understands it: set it up early and lightly, pay it off later.

## Rules, as the book shows them

### A gift both ways

*Also called: the core law, exchange, not extraction.*

> Bram restarts the falling grazers with his own old fermenters, and the grazers carry him over the ridge.

- **Costs:** Something from each side: Bram gives his baseline, his sweat, his breath; Odile gives a correct record and is marked by every biome.

### An open case freezes its evidence

*Also called: Evidence under an open case.*

> 'SUSPENDED. Conflicts with open Discrepancy. Area contains evidence.' A whole valley, saved by being entered as evidence.

- **Costs:** A formal Discrepancy goes to the Chief Examiner and stays on the Examiner's record; Odile has opened 'perhaps six' in eleven years.

### Drift and the chassis

*Also called: Law A3: life drifts without a reference, the drift, copies of copies.*

> A failing grain stalk read like a book: top pages intact, bottom pages worn like the meeting-house steps.

- **Costs:** Calibration needs an untouched copy. The cheap path drew it from Firstfield's children until they were used up; the founders' path draws it from the Library.

### Every fence leaks

*Also called: Law A2, The fence is a suggestion.*

> Where the gold grain stops at a line as straight as a knife, the wild begins anyway.

- **Costs:** Designed things escape their design: seed blows, spores drift, edit-friendly life swaps traits.

### Everything talks; everything feeds something

*Also called: Law A4, Law A5.*

> The grass says 'warm here'; the fur-trees talk about rain; the grass reads grazers as 'weather, sky, nothing'.

- **Costs:** Fix one thing and three others change; and a body that hears it all can never switch it off (root-listening, scent-speech).

### Nothing is free

*Also called: Law A1, Nothing floats for free.*

> Sky-grazers pay for their lift by fermenting seed into gas, so they must graze constantly.

- **Costs:** Every trait has a running cost in food, heat or time; every change to Bram costs hunger, cold or sleep, and none of it fully goes back.

### One reader, one Librarian

*Also called: a Librarian sleeps without a partner.*

> The Pale's Librarian tastes Bram and lets go: 'taken'.

- **Costs:** A Librarian needs a willing partner who can name things; a reader becomes, in the company's eyes, 'materials' (a living reference).

### The Choosing

*Also called: Article Fourteen, CHOOSING, CHOOSING: EXERCISED, Rumspringa clause.*

> 'And at the coming of age, each shall choose: to keep, or to go and see. And the choosing shall be theirs.'

- **Costs:** Leaving costs a family (Bram's leaving is a real loss to a loving village); keeping must be chosen, or it is captivity.

### The Reading

*Also called: Fallow's method.*

> Leave by the door you came in, or you'll leave by a window.

- **Costs:** Hours that feel like minutes; she comes out cold, stiff and starving, with a headache 'behind the eyes like a drawer slammed shut'. The Manual warns against doing it on yourself: 'no drawers there, only weather.'

### The Register's discrepancy classes

*Also called: Layer B, the six ways a record can be wrong.*

> 'Population: none' is a value and a lie; Lenna's empty 'Died' slot is an honest empty drawer.

- **Costs:** Each class is a harm someone pays for: an unrecorded valley can be burned, a misfiled network blasted, a forged index starves the plains, a retired child has no protection.

### The Third Schedule

*Also called: Hask's mandate, the Schedule, Appendix C.*

> Being shot AT is listed; being shot is not.

- **Costs:** Hask may act only to prevent an enumerated harm to the bearer; everything else is a gap he must decide about, and measurement first ('an unmeasured beast is weather').

### The symbiont can only change what is named

*Also called: Layer C, Name it and you can hold it, the symbiont's grammar.*

> He names his leg from Dr. Ommery's chart of the flayed man, the one Jory drew a moustache on.

### The heat-hunter

> It has no eyes: the soft blue bulb on its stalk, the exact colour of the singing tomatoes in the pictures, swings to follow your warmth.

- **Senses:** clicking of grey plates rubbing as it breathes / a mouth smelling hot and meaty, like the bin behind the bakehouse / hot iron and sour cheesecloth / after the flask, a scalded note on its breath

### The Dome (Firstfield's glass)

### The Heritage Primer

*Also called: the Primer.*

- **Held by:** found in the Fifth Pond's station; carried by Odile, wrapped in sailcloth

### The Register

*Also called: the Register of Moriel, the Tally's Register.*

> It chimes a double note on followed records, and the field PERSON.MAKER_LINE is 'free text... No validation is applied. Clerks need not query it.'


### The audio guide

*Also called: Lady Speaker.*

> At 3:51 in the morning, with no script, it searches and decides: 'Here we see the Baseline Human at — at — at leisure.'


### The crock

*Also called: the mother crock, the bakehouse crock, the first crock, the original crock.*

> Lift the cloth and it goes hah at you, sour and appley: if it doesn't bite you back, it's sulking.

- **Senses:** sour and yeasty and cool, like a cellar that's happy / muttering to itself in little bubbles

### The plaques

*Also called: the Wall of the Eleven, the brass plaques.*

> REFERENCE No. 12, pre-engraved by the Preserve, 'Called. [date] Retired. [blank]', found in the director's stores before the hearing.

- **Held by:** the meeting house

### The reed stem

*Also called: the knotted reed.*

> One knot a day: eight knots when Odile bags it as evidence.

- **Held by:** the first in Odile's evidence; the second with Sedge

### Varro's coat

*Also called: the colour-changing coat.*

> Grey to violet to a sort of gold as he talks, 'like a mood'.

- **Held by:** Lisle Varro

## Motifs

### Bread and the crock

*Also called: the bread.*

> Feeding the crock is Bram's job every morning since he could reach the shelf; feeding a falling grazer turns out to be the same job.


### Hands first, worry after

> The basket lands in his arms before he's finished swallowing.


### Here we see

*Also called: Note the single set of lungs.*

> 'Note,' says the audio guide, as Ma throws open the shutters, 'the single set of lungs.'


### Look twice

> Under the leaf with a hole in it, a little green caterpillar, very pleased with itself.


### Only nearly

*Also called: Not blight. Only nearly blight..*

> 'Not dead. Only nearly.'


### Shall I fix it?

> 'Your heart rate is doing something unusual near her. Shall I fix it?' 'NO.'


### Take a coat

> 'If you're going to the privy, take a coat.' 'I've got a coat.' 'So you have.'


### The Window and the fog drawing

*Also called: breathe on the glass.*

> A sun. A tomato. A face. And, at the end, a door standing open.


### The backwards B

*Also called: the B with the too-big loop.*

> His writing hand stayed his: the B with the bottom loop too big.


### The tomato joke

*Also called: What do you call a tomato that won't sing?.*

> 'A tomato.' Porridge out of the nose.


### Whose are you

*Also called: you say who you are by whose you are, Who wrote you?.*

> Bram, son of Wenna, of the house of Hale. Brother of Tilly. Grandson of Gran. And then, at the pond, he can't say it.


### Write it down

> Odile writes '13', and under it 'and more tanks', and is pleased her hand is steady.
